claim: SFFA v. Harvard/UNC (decided 2023-06-29) struck down race-conscious admissions but expressly preserved an applicant's ability to discuss race in an essay: 'nothing in this opinion should be construed as prohibiting universities from considering an applicant's discussion of how race affected his or her life, be it through discrimination, inspiration, or otherwise.' The decisive condition is that any benefit 'must be tied to that student's courage and determination' or 'unique ability to contribute to the university' — 'the student must be treated based on his or her experiences as an individual—not on the basis of race.'

application.content: When a draft mentions race or ethnicity, test it against the ruling's hinge: does the passage tie the identity to a demonstrated quality of character (courage, determination), a value, or a capacity the student will bring to campus? If the line could be cut and replaced with a bare demographic checkbox without losing anything, it is operating as a category, not an experience — rewrite it to show the specific lived moment and what it forged in the student.

BEFORE: 'As a Mexican American, diversity is important to me.' (category as standalone factor — the post-SFFA carve-out does not cover this). AFTER: a scene of teaching folklorico steps to younger cousins until the choreography finally clicked, then naming the patience and leadership it built and how that shows up in how the student runs a study group — the identity is the soil, the character quality is the fruit the reader is allowed to credit.

Only the SFFA ruling quotes in verbatimReuseOK are reproduced exactly (paraphrasing verified legal text would be a defect); everything else here is re-expressed.
